title: Building interactive fiction on a local LLM: what worked, what didn't
author: curious_biped_dev
selftext:
I'm the solo developer of s[TOR-Y]telling: Closed Loop, a Ren'Py visual novel where the AI runs entirely on the player's PC through KoboldCpp, a Llama-class model, no account, no cloud fallback. Sharing a few things from building the improv layer.

You play the narrator, the cast improvises around whatever you write, sometimes with up to nine characters answering you and each other in one scene. A few things that actually worked:

Director cues. Letting the narrator drop explicit staging instructions, not just dialogue, gives the model a clear frame to improvise inside instead of drifting.

Initiative prompting. Nudging characters to speak or act without waiting to be addressed directly is what keeps a nine-person scene from turning into a queue. Passive characters make ensemble scenes feel dead fast.

What didn't work as cleanly: sampling temperature cliffs. There's a narrow band where characters feel alive, and just outside it they either go flat and repetitive or come apart into incoherence. Finding and holding that band, especially across different characters in the same scene, took more tuning than I expected going in.

The part I'm most invested in is the Closed Loop itself: the sandbox chats aren't a side mode, they're connected to a hand-authored campaign. What you do in those sessions feeds the campaign and drives how it unfolds, its branches and its endings. I write the campaign's story and scenes, the cast's lines are generated locally.

Free demo is up on Steam if anyone wants to see how it behaves in practice: https://store.steampowered.com/app/4727010/sTORYtelling_Closed_Loop_Demo/

Happy to go deeper on any of this if useful.
